The relic cabinet

    It fills as you meet each relic, and opens in Act 7.

    Saints & Spells

    Under every saint in Sicily, the story goes, there’s a goddess wearing a disguise. We put that story on stage and checked it, claim by claim: who said it first, and what the record shows.

    A show in eight acts
    By Bryan Murphy · November 22, 2026

    • Act 1

    Scroll, and the stage changes with each act. Underlined words open a short gloss. Red stamps are myth-checks.

    Overture: under every saint, a goddess?

    You’ve probably heard some version of it. Catania’s Saint Agatha is really Isis, or Ceres. Palermo’s Saint Rosalia lives in a cave that once belonged to the Punic goddess Tanit. Scratch a Sicilian feast and you find a pagan rite underneath.

    It’s a great story. It’s also mostly a 19th-century one.

    Mulder Two thousand years of goddesses hiding in plain sight. I want to believe.

    Scully Then let’s see who said it first.

    What the record does show is stranger and better: a Church that moved into the island’s temples and calendar, and Sicilians who made its saints, relics and rites entirely their own.

    Primer: how scholars talk about this

    Syncretism. The word is Greek. Plutarch used the verb for Cretans who stopped feuding and joined forces against an outside enemy. Today it means beliefs from different sources blending into one practice.

    ”Pagan survival.” In the late 19th century, anthropologists such as Tylor treated folk customs as fossils: leftovers from an older religion, still twitching. That idea shaped how a generation read Sicily. Most scholars now reject it as a general model, though a few still argue for long continuity in particular beliefs.

    Three people to know: - Giuseppe Pitrè, in Palermo, collected Sicilian customs in 25 volumes and founded a journal for them in 1882. Palermo created the first university chair in the study of folk belief for him in 1910. He also helped start the survival story. - Antonio Gramsci, in his prison notebooks, argued that folklore was a worldview of its own, “to be taken seriously”. - Ernesto de Martino studied magic in Lucania, on the mainland, in the 1950s. He refused to call it a pre-Christian leftover and tied it to Catholic practice instead. His book Sud e magia came out in 1959.

    Scully So the man who wrote down the customs also wrote the theory about them.

    Mulder Someone has to start the file.

    Who ruled Sicily, and what they left

    Before the colonists came, the island belonged to the Sicani, the Sicels and the Elymians, with Phoenicians trading on the coasts. Greeks founded colonies from the 8th century BC.

    Then the island changed hands, again and again.

    Read it as a list
    • 535: Byzantium takes the island.
    • 831: Arabs take Palermo.
    • 1061–1091: the Normans conquer the island; Palermo falls in 1071–72.
    • 1130: Roger II is crowned, and the Kingdom of Sicily begins.
    • 1194–1266: the Hohenstaufen. 1266–1282: the Angevins.
    • 1282: the Sicilian Vespers, and Aragon takes over.
    • 1443: one king for Naples and Sicily again.
    • 1713: Savoy. 1720–1734: Austria. 1816: the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

    The Church didn’t need to hide inside the old gods. It moved into their buildings. In the late 6th century the Temple of Concord at Agrigento and the Athenaion at Syracuse became churches. Palermo’s cathedral was rebuilt, from about 1170, on the site of a mosque.

    And in 1487 the Spanish Inquisition sent its first inquisitor to Sicily. Hold that thought.

    Act 1

    Catania: Agatha goes away, and comes back

    Agatha is Catania’s own saint. About 1040, during his campaign of 1038–40, the Byzantine general George Maniakes took her body to Constantinople. No source from the time gives the year.

    Who received her there, the sources don’t agree: some say Emperor Michael IV, others Empress Theodora, who in the scholar Constantine Lascaris’s account, written some 400 years later, put the relics in a convent of virgins.

    On 17 August 1126 two soldiers, Gislebertus and Goselinus, brought it home. The clergy met it “nudis pedibus et in albis vestibus”: barefoot, in white. That makes 2026 the 900th year.

    Catania still celebrates her from 3 to 5 February, and again on 17 August for the return. Devotees wear a white robe, the . One story says it recalls the nightshirts people ran out in when the relics came home in 1126. The historian Benigno says the robe is an 18th-century creation.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: the remembers 1126What the record shows: no historical support

    Her silver bust was made by Giovanni di Bartolo of Siena; its inscription dates it to 1376. Her crown is not a gift from Richard the Lionheart, whatever you’ve heard: it was made in the late 15th century.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Richard the Lionheart’s crownWhat the record shows: made in the late 1400s

    Devotees hold that her veil protects the city from Etna’s lava. When Etna erupted in 1669 the veil was carried in processions from March to July; the lava reached Catania on 30 April.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Agatha is Ceres in disguiseWhat the record shows: first claimed 1823

    The English writer J. J. Blunt said it first, and admitted he couldn’t prove it. The Isis version comes from Emanuele Ciaceri in 1905. A 2025 study’s title says it plainly: “Né Demetra, né Iside” (neither Demeter nor Isis).

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: “the world’s third-largest religious festival”What the record shows: no source found

    Mulder A saint who stops a volcano.

    Scully A city that walked into the lava’s path carrying her veil. Both of those are true.

    Act 2

    Palermo: Rosalia and the plague

    In May 1624 the plague reached Palermo.

    Rosalia was a local hermit of the 12th century, as tradition tells it, with a small cult and not much else.

    Then, on 15 July 1624, bones were found in a cave on Monte Pellegrino. Tradition says the visions of a sick woman, Geronima La Gattuta of Ciminna, led the search.

    Here is the timeline, and it is the punchline.

    Read it as a list
    • 15 July 1624: bones found.
    • 27 July 1624: the Senate elects Rosalia patron of Palermo.
    • November 1624: the Church sets up a commission to check whether the bones are hers.
    • February 1625: the commission says yes.
    • 9 June 1625: the relics’ first procession.
    • 15 July 1625: the plague is declared over, one year to the day after the finding.

    The cathedral’s own account adds one more vision. On 4 February 1625 a soap-maker, Vincenzo Bonelli (some spell it Bonello), climbed Monte Pellegrino meaning to kill himself. He said Rosalia appeared to him there and asked for a procession of her relics.

    Palermo made her its patron seven months before anyone confirmed whose bones they were. Palermitans credit her with ending the plague; that is their belief, and they have kept it for four centuries.

    A Life of Rosalia came out in 1627, and her name entered the Roman Martyrology about 1630. Her relics have lain in a silver urn in the cathedral since 1631.

    Even so, she never took over the island. Around 1900 the folklorist Pitrè surveyed about 150 towns: Mary was the main patron of 45, the Crucifix of 13, and Rosalia of 7.

    Today the runs 10 to 15 July, with the great cart on the evening of the 14th and the urn procession on the 15th. The 400th festino was in 2024. On the night of 3 to 4 September comes the , the climb up the mountain to her cave.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Rosalia’s cave was Tanit’s shrineWhat the record shows: no finds, no inscription

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: a geologist proved the bones were a goat’sWhat the record shows: a late, second-hand anecdote

    Scully Elected first, authenticated later.

    Mulder And the plague still ended. Just saying.

    Act 3

    Messina: a letter from Mary

    Messina’s feast on 3 June honors a letter. The legend says the Virgin Mary wrote to the people of Messina in the year 42, from Jerusalem, and tied the letter with a lock of her hair.

    The legend arose in the 16th century. The oldest manuscript copy is from 1599.

    In 1629 a scholar named Inchofer published a defense of the letter. The Church’s own censors, the Congregation of the Index, objected; a corrected edition came out in 1632.

    The hair relic still rides the city’s silver in procession.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: found in Greek and translated in the 1400sWhat the record shows: the supporters’ claim, unsupported

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: “venerated since the Middle Ages”What the record shows: oldest firm date: 1522

    Mulder A letter from the Virgin Mary.

    Scully Censored by the Vatican for overselling it.

    Act 4

    St Joseph’s tables

    On 19 March, Joseph’s feast, Sicilian families build tables of bread and food and feed three of the poorest people they can find, often children, dressed as Mary, Joseph and Jesus: the .

    The night before, bonfires: the .

    Pitrè recorded these meals for the poor by 1900 at the latest. Nobody knows exactly when they began. The folklorist Del Giudice found nothing like them in Spain or its colonies.

    In the Sicilian Region’s register of living traditions, as it stood in 2013, St Joseph had 11 of its 86 celebrations, more than any other saint.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: a medieval famine ended by fava beansWhat the record shows: told mostly by emigrants, with no source

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: a Christianized Demeter riteWhat the record shows: parallels, not descent

    Mulder Feeding the poor as if they were the Holy Family.

    Scully No myth required.

    Act 5 · night

    The dead come back

    In Palermo, by the Oreto river, a church honors the : the beheaded, executed criminals whom devotees believe can intercede for the living. The church was rebuilt in 1785 and again later; executed people were buried there. In Pitrè’s day its walls held about a hundred painted tablets of thanks, by his own count.

    In 1817 a man named Francesco Frusteri was beheaded at Paceco, and people made him a popular saint.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: a pagan survivalWhat the record shows: Pitrè read it as a Christian idea: the repentant executed as martyrs

    On 2 November, the Day of the Dead, Sicilian families say the dead come back and leave gifts for the children: sugar dolls, fruit and nuts in a basket.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: nuns invented marzipan fruit for a visiting archbishopWhat the record shows: no document found

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: the gifts continue Roman offeringsWhat the record shows: no named source

    An ex-voto is a thank-you made visible. Painted ones show the danger, the person saved and the holy helper; wax, metal or terracotta ones show the healed body part. The Palermo scholar I. E. Buttitta calls a painted ex-voto a “standing declaration of debt” to the saint.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: ex-votos prove a pagan lineWhat the record shows: resemblance, not descent

    Act 6 · night

    Witches, healers and the evil eye

    From 1487 to 1782, Sicily had its own court of the Spanish Inquisition, answering to Madrid, not Rome. From 1601 it sat in the Steri palace in Palermo. Its archive was burned in 1783.

    The numbers: it tried about 6,000 to 7,000 people. About 1,000 were charged with magic or witchcraft. Between 1540 and 1700 it executed 25 to 52 people in person, for any charge, and almost no one for witchcraft. No woman is known to have been executed as a witch.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: “thousands of witches burned in Sicily”What the record shows: two men handed over in nearly three centuries

    The ladies from outside. Dozens of people stood trial for dealing with the . They were above all healers: people went to them to cure illnesses the fairies were said to have caused.

    The historian Gustav Henningsen read the trials as a Sicilian fairy cult with a “white” sabbath, a shared set of cultural dreams. Was it shamanism? Henningsen says no, because no trance technique is described; others still compare it to shamanic cults.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: an unbroken pagan cult from antiquityWhat the record shows: the trials show a 16th–17th-century cult, nothing older

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: the magic trials were all about womenWhat the record shows: men were tried too, and the only two handed over for witchcraft were men

    The evil eye. Sicilians call it or . It isn’t only Sicilian: belief in it runs across southern Europe.

    Healers still lift it. Between 2002 and 2006 the researcher Napoli met about 25 , worm-charmers, in five provinces. They make three crosses on the stomach while reciting charms that run through Holy Week, day by day, “cutting” the worms. They also lift the evil eye, with a little plate, .

    Against it, English collectors in the early 1900s recorded coral, silver-bell rattles, the charm and the raised thumb and little finger, as a 2025 Palermo University Press study reports.

    Mulder Fairy women who cure the sick.

    Scully The Inquisition’s own records say so. That’s the strange part.

    Act 7

    The relic cabinet opens

    How many fingerbones can one dead saint have? In Sicily’s case, the honest answer is disappointing: we found no saint with two of the same finger.

    What we did find:

    • Lucy’s body: two places claim the whole thing, Venice and Metz. Syracuse, where she was buried, has the empty tomb.
    • Lucy’s head: Venice and Bourges each have a claim, by our own comparison of the sources.
    • Agatha: spread, not doubled. One tourism list names 31 places outside Catania with a piece of her, and where parts can be counted, the numbers add up. Palermo Cathedral holds her arm.
    • Louis IX of France, who died on crusade at Tunis in 1270: his entrails, and by one medieval account his heart, were buried at Monreale.

    Palermo Cathedral says its Chapel of the Relics holds 17 reliquaries. No one has counted them for the island.

    The critics. In 1543 John Calvin wrote a Treatise on Relics. Collect every piece of the True Cross, he joked, and you’d fill a good big boat. Every apostle had more than four bodies, and each saint at least two or three.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Calvin counted a dozen heads of John the BaptistWhat the record shows: that was his translator

    The rules. Canon law says: “It is absolutely forbidden to sell sacred relics.” The Vatican’s 2017 rules ban trading them too, and forbid cutting up a saint’s body without Rome’s consent.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: first-, second- and third-class relics are Church lawWhat the record shows: not in the current rules

    Act 8

    To the Americas

    Sicily and Latin America both love candles and baroque gold. Is there a real connection? Some, through one empire.

    Benedict the Moor. Born at San Fratello to African parents who had been enslaved, he died at a convent in Palermo on 4 April 1589. He was beatified in 1743 and made a saint in 1807.

    His cult traveled with Black Catholic brotherhoods: a confraternity in Lisbon by 1609, and across Brazil and the Spanish and Portuguese New World from the early 1600s. In Venezuela his feast is danced to the chimbangueles drums.

    Antonio of Noto, another Sicilian holy man honored by the same brotherhoods, died at Noto in 1549 or 1550. In Brazil he is still venerated as Santo Antônio de Categeró.

    Rosalia crossed to New Spain with the Jesuits and the Spanish crown’s networks. And in 1555 the first Mexican Church council made Saint Joseph patron of “this new Church”.

    The shared look, the candles and the gold? No scholar we found traces it to one source. Votive candles are a habit of Catholics everywhere, and the baroque turned up the volume in both places.

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Mexico got the Day of the Dead from SicilyWhat the record shows: no transfer found either way

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: Sicilian immigrants carried these saints to Argentina, Brazil and VenezuelaWhat the record shows: they went earlier, through Spain and Portugal

    Myth-check

    Myth-check. Claim: St Joseph’s tables are a Latin American tradition tooWhat the record shows: not found

    Mulder Two Sicilian saints in the drums of Venezuela.

    Scully Carried by Black brotherhoods through Lisbon, not by emigrants.

    Curtain call

    The goddesses under the saints are mostly stories from the 1800s. What’s real is better: a Church that moved into Sicily’s temples and calendar, and Sicilians who made it their own, with a hermit elected patron before her bones were checked, a letter from Mary, tables for the poor, gifts from the dead, and healers the Inquisition couldn’t quite bring itself to burn.

    Mulder I still want to believe.

    Scully Good. Now you know what you’re believing.

    About these numbers

    Every number on this page comes from a table of checked figures. The research ran as many independent passes (different searches, different sources) whose results were cross-checked against each other: each figure needed two independent sources, preferably the original institution, book or journal. Where sources disagree, the page shows a range or names the disagreement: 1071–72 for Palermo’s fall, “about 1040” for Agatha’s removal, about 6,000 to 7,000 people tried, 25 to 52 executions.

    “Dozens tried” for the donne di fuora is deliberate: counts run from 65 to 77 to 193, depending on what is counted (people in the surviving reports, one historian’s charges of contact with the dead, perhaps every woman named). Counts that come from a single document name that document in the sentence: Pitrè’s survey, the Sicilian Region’s 2013 register, Pitrè’s tally of painted tablets, Napoli’s worm-charmers, the collectors in Intorre’s study, Palermo Cathedral’s 17 reliquaries. The relic drawers are what the sources report, not an inventory; “two claims” for Lucy’s body and head is our own comparison. No survey of evil-eye belief in Sicily turned up, so the page says nothing about how many Sicilians hold it today. Beliefs are written as beliefs.

    The myth-check stamps mark claims that circulate widely and that the record does not support. A stamp means “no evidence found”, never “proven false”, unless it says so.

    Pictures

    • Saint Rosalia: Anthony van Dyck, Saint Rosalie Interceding for the Plague-stricken of Palermo, 1624 (detail). The Met, 71.41. CC0.
    • Rosalia’s car: Jean Houël, The car of Saint Rosalia, aquatint, 1780s. Wellcome Collection, 7145i. Public Domain Mark.
    • Saint Agatha: Saint Agatha, bronze statuette, Italian (probably Naples), mid-17th c. The Met, 197071. CC0.
    • A reliquary bust: Reliquary Bust of Saint Juliana, circle of Giovanni di Bartolo, c. 1376. The Met, 61.266. CC0. A stand-in: Agatha’s own bust in Catania is by Giovanni di Bartolo.
    • Saint Lucy: Francisco de Zurbarán, Saint Lucy, c. 1625/30. National Gallery of Art, 1943.7.11. Public domain.
    • Saint Joseph: St. Joseph, crèche figure, attributed to Salvatore di Franco, Naples, 2nd half 18th c. The Met, 64.164.3a–c. CC0.
    • A goddess: Terracotta bust (Persephone or Demeter), Greek, made in Sicily, 4th c. BCE. The Met, 1994.600.1–.2. CC0.
    • Isis: Statuette of Isis nursing Horus, Egyptian, Late Period, 664–332 BCE. The Met, 553002. CC0.
    • A Palermo jar: Albarello (pharmacy jar), Lazzaro workshop, Palermo, 2nd half 16th c. The Met, 188537. CC0. Its foliage also makes the tile wall.
    • The proscenium: Gilt ripple frame, Sicilian(?), late 17th c. The Met, 1975.1.2326. CC0.
    • An ex-voto: Ex-voto: a man falls in a Roman street while his wife prays to Sansovino’s Virgin and Child, 27 May 1851. Rome, not Sicily. Wellcome Collection, 44879i. Public Domain Mark.
    • An angel: Angel, crèche figure, Naples, 2nd half 18th c. The Met (crèche angels, 64.164). CC0.
    • Drawn for this page: the scholars’ and rulers’ placards, the boat, the letter, the table, the ship the blue glass eye charm and the coral horn charm. No open-licensed picture of Benedict the Moor or Antonio of Noto turned up, so they are not shown.
